source.title: Feature survival under weight pruning: Sparse autoencoder diagnostics for compressed language models
source.authors: Hector Borobia; Elies Seguí-Mas; Guillermina Tormo Carbó

record.file_problem: The supplied metadata title differs from the title printed in the paper; the text is a full paper about SAE features under weight pruning, not an apparent wrong document.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE feature matching and survival across dense and weight-pruned models, but does not test whether increasing SAE dictionary size splits coarse features into finer ones.
record.gate_note: The reported MNN and firing-rate survival results concern feature correspondence under weight pruning, not splitting caused by SAE dictionary growth. SAE reconstruction and ablation results do not test the listed versions either.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs of one fixed width (8× d_model, k=64) on dense and weight-pruned models and matches features across pruning conditions. It runs no dictionary-size sweep and no parent/child or hierarchy analysis, and compares no training objectives. None of its results bear on whether features split as dictionaries grow, absorb, decompose across sizes, or arise from the sparsity objective.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Rare SAE features survive pruning better than frequent ones, and Wanda preserves feature structure better than magnitude pruning. Dense-trained SAEs stay usable on Wanda-pruned models up to 50% sparsity. Geometric survival does not predict causal importance. Nothing is concluded about splitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study matches SAE features across dense and weight-pruned models rather than training SAEs of increasing dictionary size on the same activations. It studies pruning effects, not feature splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature matching and survival vary with pruning method, sparsity, model, and firing-rate quintile.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense-to-pruned SAE feature survival (MNN, τ=0.7) depends on pruning method and sparsity. Wanda exceeds magnitude pruning, e.g. Gemma 2 at 30%: 0.794 vs 0.213.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning method and sparsity determine how much SAE feature geometry survives weight pruning.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-firing-rate SAE features survive pruning better than high-firing-rate ones (ρ=−1.0 in 11 of 17 conditions).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature survival under pruning is negatively associated with firing rate.

record.problems: All models are in the 1–2B parameter range; the paper notes low absolute seed-to-seed MNN rates (2–4%) and that specific robust or fragile features may depend on seed. These results do not address dictionary-size splitting.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted SAE seed-stability measurements, official-SAE transferability/FVU, causal ablation KL values, pruning perplexity, and predictive-model results: these concern seed reproducibility, reconstruction, causal relevance, task quality, or prediction rather than the feature correspondence and survival results catalogued here (Sections 4.1, 4.4, 4.6–4.7; Tables 1, 2, and 4).

untested.parts: All: no SAE width sweep; only one expansion factor is used.
All: no dictionary-size splitting in large models or open SAE releases. Gemma Scope SAEs are used only for reconstruction FVU.
All: no feature families or hierarchy analysis.
All: no parent/child firing or absorption measure.
All: no cross-size latent decomposition or novel-latent test.
All: no comparison of SAE objectives. Low seed-to-seed MNN (1.1–3.9%) is reported but not tied to splitting.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked (versions none). The paper cites Towards Monosemanticity only as background. Seed instability is attributed to many equivalent sparse decompositions at large width, but this is not tested against dictionary size.

versions.untested_parts: No SAE dictionary-size sweep or test that finer features partition a coarse feature's inputs or lie near its direction.
No test of dictionary-size splitting in large models or open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families or whether they mirror a conceptual hierarchy.
No parent-child feature firing or splitting test; no comparison of size or sparsity as a remedy for absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, nor test for novel latents across SAE dictionary sizes.
No comparison of SAE objectives or test of whether the training objective produces feature splitting.
